lesson.title: Undoing Exponential Growth: Logarithmic Functions as Inverses
lesson.summary: This section defines the logarithmic function as the inverse of the exponential function, covers its core properties, and solves two equations, one using logarithms to undo an exponential and one using logarithm properties to solve an equation with a logarithm in it.
lesson.body:
The exponential function b^x answers the question: what do I get if I raise b to the x power. The logarithmic function answers the reverse question: what power do I need to raise b to, in order to get this number. Formally, for a base b with b > 0 and b not equal to 1, y = log_b(x) means exactly the same thing as b^y = x. This makes the logarithm the inverse function of the exponential function with the same base, in precisely the sense already developed for inverse functions generally: log_b and the exponential b^x undo each other, so b^(log_b(x)) = x and log_b(b^x) = x.

Because inverses swap domain and range, and the exponential function b^x has domain all real numbers and range restricted to positive numbers only, the logarithmic function log_b(x) has domain restricted to positive numbers only and range all real numbers. This is worth remembering as a hard rule: log_b(x) is simply undefined whenever x is zero or negative, no matter what base is used.

Three algebraic properties make logarithms useful for solving equations: log_b(mn) = log_b(m) + log_b(n), turning multiplication into addition; log_b(m/n) = log_b(m) - log_b(n), turning division into subtraction; and log_b(m^p) = p*log_b(m), pulling an exponent down in front as a multiplier. These properties follow directly from the corresponding exponent rules, since logarithms and exponents are inverse operations of each other.

These properties solve equations that would otherwise be very difficult. Consider log_3(x) + log_3(x-2) = 1. Using the product rule in reverse, combine the left side into a single logarithm: log_3[x(x-2)] = 1. Converting to exponential form using the definition of logarithm, x(x-2) = 3^1 = 3, which expands to x^2 - 2x - 3 = 0, factoring as (x-3)(x+1) = 0, giving candidate solutions x = 3 and x = -1. But x = -1 must be rejected: log_3(x) requires x > 0, and this candidate fails that requirement immediately. Checking x = 3 in the original equation: log_3(3) + log_3(1) = 1 + 0 = 1, which is correct, so x = 3 is the only valid solution.

Logarithms are also the standard tool for solving an exponential equation where the variable sits in the exponent. To solve 2^x = 20 for x, take the logarithm of both sides: x = log_2(20). Using the change of base formula, log_2(20) = ln(20)/ln(2), which evaluates to approximately 2.9957/0.6931, or about 4.3219. Checking this is reasonable: 2^4 = 16 and 2^5 = 32, and 20 sits between them, closer to 16, so an exponent a little above 4 makes sense.
